Indolent

IN-duh-lent · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Indolent is wanting to avoid activity or exertion.

The cat spent the entire afternoon in an indolent sprawl across the windowsill, ignoring every toy we dangled in front of it.

Worked Example

Despite his coach's warnings, the indolent player skipped every optional practice all season and was benched by playoffs.

Indolent describes a habitual preference for avoiding effort, not a single tired afternoon.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

lazy: Lazy is the everyday word for avoiding work or effort, at home in any casual complaint. Indolent means the same fault in formal dress: laziness as a settled, habitual way of life rather than a passing mood.

idle: Idle describes the state of simply not doing anything at the moment — idle machines, idle hands, an idle afternoon — and it may be nobody's fault at all. Indolent is a character trait: a person who, day after day, chooses to avoid effort itself.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

industrious: hardworking and diligent

energetic: full of energy and enthusiasm

Where it sits · how routinely work gets dodged — relaxed → indolent → slothful

relaxed vs. indolent: Relaxed is much milder than indolent: taking one lazy Sunday off is relaxed, while an indolent person goes further, dodging work and effort itself week after week.

slothful vs. indolent: Slothful goes a step beyond indolent: an indolent person dodges effort whenever possible, while slothful condemns a deeper, almost total idleness — the old word for laziness as a vice.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — in-

prefix — in-: not (Latin)

root+suffix — dolent

root+suffix — dolent: feeling pain or grief (Latin (dolere))

Put it together

Put it together: in- ("not") + dolent ("feeling pain") = literally "feeling no pain" -- originally, avoiding effort so as not to suffer, which gave us today's sense of "lazy."

Use the root in a new word: dolorous

Use the root in a new word: dolorous: The same root survives in the rarer word "dolorous," meaning full of sorrow or grief.
